qsradiologicalfindinginthyrotoxicosis.exp: Radioiodine uptake is increased in thyrotoxicosis caused by increased hormone synthesis and decreased in thyroiditis. Thyroid scintigraphy distinguishes the pattern: diffuse uptake suggests Graves disease, a solitary hot nodule suggests a toxic adenoma, and multiple areas of uptake suggest toxic multinodular goiter.

a38yoldladynoticedthatsheislosingweighta.exp:
a. Diagnosis: thyrotoxicosis, most likely Graves' disease (weight loss, anxiety, insomnia, marked tachycardia and warm tremulous hands); the normal ESR and normal temperature argue against subacute (de Quervain's) thyroiditis.
b. Investigations: TSH (suppressed), free T4 and free T3 (raised); TSH-receptor antibodies; radioactive iodine uptake scan (diffuse high uptake in Graves', low in thyroiditis) and thyroid ultrasound with Doppler; ECG (sinus tachycardia or atrial fibrillation); CBC and liver functions as baseline.
c. Treatment: propranolol for symptomatic control; carbimazole/methimazole (e.g. 20-40 mg/day, then titrated) for 12-18 months, with counselling about agranulocytosis; radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy for relapse, large goitre or intolerance of drugs; regular thyroid function follow-up.

a22yoldfemalestudentsufferedfromiddmfort.exp:
a. Possible causes of tachycardia, sweating and nervousness in a type 1 diabetic: hypoglycaemia (insulin overdose, missed meals, exercise); thyrotoxicosis (Graves' disease or Hashitoxicosis - autoimmune thyroid disease is associated with type 1 DM); diabetic autonomic neuropathy (resting tachycardia); anxiety state; pheochromocytoma (rare); drugs (e.g. beta-agonists, excessive caffeine).
b. Hypoglycaemia (example): diagnosis by Whipple's triad - symptoms, low blood glucose (below 70 mg/dl, adrenergic symptoms like tachycardia, sweating, tremor and nervousness, and neuroglycopenic symptoms) and relief after glucose; check capillary glucose during symptoms and review insulin doses and HbA1c. Management: if conscious give 15-20 g rapid oral glucose and recheck after 15 min, then a complex carbohydrate snack; if unconscious give IV 50 ml of 50% dextrose (or 20% dextrose) or IM glucagon 1 mg; then adjust insulin regimen, regular meals and snacks, glucose monitoring, education of patient and family, carry sugar and a diabetic card. (Alternatively thyrotoxicosis: TSH, free T4/T3, TRAb; treat with beta-blocker and carbimazole.)

35yearsoldfemalesufferfromparoxysmalhtna.exp:
a. Diagnosis: pheochromocytoma (paroxysmal hypertension with attacks of headache, sweating, palpitation, pallor and anxiety, plus weight loss, heat intolerance and constipation from catecholamine excess).
b. Investigations: biochemical confirmation by plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines (VMA less sensitive); blood glucose (hyperglycaemia); localisation by CT or MRI of the adrenals/abdomen, then MIBG or PET scan for extra-adrenal or metastatic disease; screening for associated syndromes (MEN 2 - serum calcitonin, calcium and PTH; von Hippel-Lindau, NF1) and genetic testing.
c. Treatment: preoperative alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 10-14 days with high salt and fluid intake, then a beta-blocker added only after adequate alpha-blockade; surgical removal by laparoscopic adrenalectomy with careful anaesthesia (control of hypertensive crisis by IV phentolamine or nitroprusside, and postoperative hypotension/hypoglycaemia by fluids and glucose); for inoperable or malignant disease, alpha-methyl-para-tyrosine, MIBG therapy or chemotherapy; long-term follow-up with metanephrines.

a64yearsoldmannoticedthathehadgained8kgi.exp:
a. Provisional diagnosis: Cushing's syndrome (weight gain with central obesity, easy bruising, purple striae, proximal myopathy, depression, hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance); in a 64-year-old man ectopic ACTH secretion (e.g. from a lung tumour) must be considered besides pituitary Cushing's disease, adrenal tumour and exogenous steroid intake.
b. Investigation: exclude exogenous glucocorticoid use; confirm hypercortisolism with 24-hour urinary free cortisol, overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test and late-night salivary cortisol (two positive tests); then plasma ACTH - suppressed (adrenal adenoma/carcinoma: CT adrenals) or normal/raised (ACTH-dependent: high-dose dexamethasone suppression and CRH tests, pituitary MRI, inferior petrosal sinus sampling, and CT chest/abdomen for an ectopic source); also serum potassium, blood glucose/OGTT, DEXA scan. Management: transsphenoidal adenomectomy for Cushing's disease (radiotherapy or bilateral adrenalectomy if it fails); unilateral adrenalectomy for an adrenal adenoma; resection of the ectopic tumour; medical cortisol-lowering drugs (metyrapone, ketoconazole, osilodrostat, mifepristone) before surgery or if inoperable; treat hypertension, diabetes, hypokalaemia and osteoporosis; postoperative hydrocortisone replacement until the HPA axis recovers.

awoman44yoldcomplainingofincreasingweakn.exp:
a. Diagnosis: primary hypothyroidism (markedly raised TSH with weakness, constipation, pallor, puffy eyelids and bradycardia), most likely autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis.
b. Explanation: failure of the thyroid gland lowers T4/T3, removing negative feedback so pituitary TSH rises greatly. Thyroid hormone deficiency reduces metabolic rate and sympathetic sensitivity (bradycardia, weakness), slows gut motility (constipation), causes accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the tissues (myxoedema: puffy eyelids) and anaemia plus skin vasoconstriction and carotenaemia (pallor).
c. Treatment: levothyroxine daily on an empty stomach, starting at a moderate dose (lower if elderly or cardiac) and titrating. Follow-up: TSH (with free T4) 6-8 weeks after each dose change, aiming for TSH within the normal range, then every 6-12 months; clinical review of symptoms, weight, pulse and anaemia.

malepatient65yearsoldrecentlysufferedfro.exp:
a. Differential diagnosis: Cushing's syndrome (truncal obesity, diabetes, hypertension and proximal myopathy) complicated by an osteoporotic vertebral collapse fracture after minor trauma. Causes to differentiate: exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoid intake; ACTH-dependent - pituitary Cushing's disease and ectopic ACTH secretion (e.g. small cell lung carcinoma, especially in a 65-year-old man); ACTH-independent adrenal adenoma or carcinoma. Other causes of back pain: vertebral metastases (e.g. from lung or prostate cancer), multiple myeloma, traumatic fracture.
b. Investigations: screening - 24-hour urinary free cortisol, overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol; then plasma ACTH (suppressed = adrenal; normal/high = pituitary or ectopic), high-dose dexamethasone suppression and CRH tests, pituitary MRI, adrenal CT, chest CT for an ectopic source, inferior petrosal sinus sampling; serum potassium (hypokalaemia in ectopic ACTH), blood glucose/HbA1c; spine X-ray/MRI and DEXA scan for the fracture and osteoporosis.
c. Treatment: treat the cause - transsphenoidal pituitary surgery, adrenalectomy, or removal of the ectopic tumour; withdraw exogenous steroids gradually; medical control of cortisol (ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat) when surgery is delayed or not possible; control of diabetes, hypertension and hypokalaemia; for the fracture - analgesia, rest/brace, calcium, vitamin D and bisphosphonates; postoperative glucocorticoid replacement until the axis recovers.

a. Other symptoms to ask about: failure of lactation after delivery; loss of axillary and pubic hair; loss of libido, breast atrophy; symptoms of hypothyroidism (cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain, dry skin, slowness); symptoms of adrenal insufficiency (fatigue, anorexia, nausea, weight loss, postural dizziness, hypoglycaemic attacks); pallor (skin depigmentation) and loss of energy; polyuria is rare.
b. Diagnosis: Sheehan's syndrome - postpartum ischaemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary causing hypopituitarism (panhypopituitarism).
c. Investigations: basal hormones - low FSH/LH with low oestradiol; low free T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH; low 8 a.m. cortisol with low ACTH and poor response to the Synacthen or insulin tolerance test; low prolactin and IGF-1; stimulation (combined pituitary function) tests; serum sodium and glucose; MRI of the pituitary (empty sella).
d. Treatment: hormone replacement - hydrocortisone first (before thyroxine, to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis), then levothyroxine (monitor free T4, not TSH), then oestrogen/progestogen replacement (gonadotrophins if fertility is desired), growth hormone if indicated; steroid card and sick-day rules.
e. Prognosis: good with adequate lifelong replacement and patient education; risk of adrenal crisis and death with stress, infection or surgery if steroid cover is not increased; the pituitary damage is permanent.

a. Differential diagnosis of coma in a type 1 diabetic boy: hypoglycaemic coma; diabetic ketoacidosis; (rarely) hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state or lactic acidosis; non-diabetic causes - head injury, meningitis/encephalitis, cerebral oedema, drug or alcohol intoxication, epilepsy (post-ictal).
b. Investigations: immediate bedside capillary glucose; then laboratory blood glucose, blood or urine ketones, arterial/venous blood gases (pH, bicarbonate, anion gap), serum sodium and potassium, urea and creatinine, serum osmolality, CBC and cultures for infection, urine analysis; CT brain and CSF examination if metabolic causes are excluded.
c. Management of the above: hypoglycaemia - IV 50 ml of 50% (or 2-5 ml/kg of 10%) dextrose or IM glucagon, followed by a dextrose infusion and oral carbohydrate on waking, then review of insulin dose and meals. DKA - isotonic saline for rehydration, IV regular insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/h, potassium replacement according to serum K, add dextrose when glucose falls to about 250 mg/dl, bicarbonate only if pH below 6.9, treat the precipitating infection, and monitor glucose, electrolytes, pH and watch for cerebral oedema.

a. Provisional diagnosis: hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS; non-ketotic hyperosmolar coma) in a newly presenting type 2 diabetic - elderly patient, very high glucose (684 mg/dl), severe dehydration (haemoconcentration: Hb 16, hematocrit 50; prerenal azotaemia: BUN 46, creatinine 1.8) with normal bicarbonate (no significant acidosis).
b. Investigations to confirm: serum osmolality (measured or calculated = 2 Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8; above 320 mOsm/kg); serum sodium and potassium; blood/urine ketones (absent or mild); arterial blood gases (pH above 7.30, bicarbonate above 18 mmol/L); renal function; HbA1c; search for precipitating factors - CBC, blood and urine cultures, chest X-ray, ECG and cardiac enzymes, CT brain if focal signs.
c. Line of treatment: IV fluid replacement is the priority - 0.9% saline 1-1.5 L in the first hour, then guided by sodium and osmolality (0.45% saline if corrected sodium is high), replacing the deficit gradually over 24-48 h; low-dose IV insulin (about 0.05-0.1 unit/kg/h) started after fluids have begun to lower glucose, aiming at a slow fall; add 5% dextrose when glucose falls to about 300 mg/dl; potassium replacement; prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin (thrombosis risk); treat the precipitating cause (infection); monitor glucose, electrolytes, osmolality, urine output and neurological status; later long-term diabetes management (often oral agents or insulin).

gravesdisease1rythyrotoxicosisdefineclin.exp: Graves disease is autoimmune primary hyperthyroidism caused by TSH-receptor-stimulating antibodies. Symptoms include heat intolerance, sweating, weight loss despite appetite, palpitations, tremor, anxiety, frequent stools and menstrual disturbance. Signs include diffuse goiter with bruit, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, warm moist skin, fine tremor, lid retraction/stare and, in Graves disease, ophthalmopathy or pretibial dermopathy. TSH is suppressed with raised free T4 and/or T3; TSH-receptor antibodies support the diagnosis. If needed, uptake is diffusely increased; ultrasound shows diffuse enlargement and hypervascularity. Relieve adrenergic symptoms with a beta blocker; control hormone synthesis with methimazole (PTU is preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy). Definitive options are radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy, selected for the patient and disease; monitor thyroid function and treat resulting hypothyroidism.

thyrotoxicosiscausessymptomsspecificclin.exp: Thyrotoxicosis is excess circulating thyroid hormone. Causes include Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis (subacute, painless or postpartum), excess iodine/amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone, hCG-mediated disease, a TSH-secreting pituitary tumor, struma ovarii and functioning metastases. Symptoms: heat intolerance, sweating, weight loss, palpitations, tremor, anxiety, proximal weakness and increased bowel frequency. Signs: tachycardia/atrial fibrillation, warm moist skin, fine tremor, hyperreflexia and goiter; Graves may add eye signs and pretibial dermopathy. Confirm with suppressed TSH and raised free T4 and/or T3. Use TSH-receptor antibodies for Graves; uptake/scintigraphy distinguishes diffuse Graves uptake, focal toxic nodules and low-uptake thyroiditis or exogenous hormone. Treat the cause: beta blocker for symptoms; antithyroid drugs for hormone synthesis; radioactive iodine or surgery for Graves/autonomous nodules when appropriate; thyroiditis is generally treated symptomatically, not with thionamides.

definesubclinicalhypothyroidism.exp: Subclinical hypothyroidism is a raised serum TSH with free T4 within the reference range (usually with no or mild symptoms). It may be transient or reflect early autoimmune thyroiditis, prior thyroid treatment, iodine imbalance or a drug effect. Confirm with repeat TSH/free T4 and assess thyroid peroxidase antibodies and symptoms. Consider levothyroxine when TSH is persistently at least 10 mIU/L, or at lower elevations in selected symptomatic patients, pregnancy/planning pregnancy, positive TPO antibodies, goiter or relevant cardiovascular risk. Otherwise monitor TSH and free T4 periodically. Recheck TSH about 6–8 weeks after starting or changing levothyroxine.

subacutethyroiditisdequervanthyroiditisc.exp: Subacute (De Quervain) thyroiditis is a usually post-viral, painful inflammatory thyroiditis. It causes fever, malaise and a tender enlarged thyroid with pain that may radiate to the jaw or ear; a transient thyrotoxic phase may be followed by temporary hypothyroidism and then recovery. Early tests show suppressed TSH and raised free T4/T3; ESR/CRP are elevated and radioactive iodine uptake is low. Treat pain/inflammation with an NSAID; use corticosteroids for severe or persistent pain. A beta blocker can control thyrotoxic symptoms. Antithyroid drugs are not useful because hormone excess is from leakage, not increased synthesis. Give temporary levothyroxine if the hypothyroid phase is symptomatic or prolonged, with follow-up thyroid function tests.

comparebetweengravesdiseasetoxicmultinod.exp: Graves disease is autoimmune and commonly affects younger adults; toxic multinodular goiter is more common in older people and often follows longstanding nodular goiter. Graves produces a diffuse, smooth goiter, sometimes with bruit, ophthalmopathy and pretibial dermopathy; toxic multinodular goiter has an irregular nodular gland and no characteristic Graves eye/skin disease. Both suppress TSH and raise free T4 and/or T3. TSH-receptor antibodies are usually positive in Graves and negative in toxic multinodular goiter. Radioiodine uptake is diffusely increased in Graves and patchy/heterogeneous with autonomous nodules in toxic multinodular goiter; ultrasound shows diffuse hypervascularity versus multiple nodules. Treatment options include antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine or surgery, individualized to cause, age, comorbidity, goiter size and patient preference.

cancerthyroiddiscussriskfactorforfromthe.exp: Thyroid cancer risk clues include childhood head/neck irradiation, a first-degree relative with thyroid cancer, familial medullary cancer or MEN2, and relevant inherited syndromes. Concerning history/examination includes a rapidly enlarging, hard or fixed nodule, hoarseness, dysphagia, compressive symptoms, cervical lymphadenopathy or vocal-cord palsy. Evaluate with TSH and high-quality thyroid/neck ultrasound, including cervical nodes; perform ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration when sonographic pattern and nodule size meet criteria. If TSH is low, radionuclide scanning identifies a functioning nodule, which is rarely malignant. Cytology guides surveillance, repeat sampling or surgery. For suspected medullary cancer, measure calcitonin and evaluate for RET/MEN2 as indicated.

solitarythyroidnoduletheapproachestodiag.exp: For a solitary thyroid nodule, take a history of growth, radiation exposure, family history, hoarseness and compressive symptoms; examine the thyroid, cervical nodes and voice. Measure TSH and perform thyroid/neck ultrasound to characterize the nodule and lymph nodes. If TSH is suppressed, obtain radionuclide scintigraphy: a hyperfunctioning nodule rarely needs cytology, while nonfunctioning nodules are assessed by ultrasound risk and size. Perform ultrasound-guided FNA when indicated and manage according to cytology (Bethesda): observe benign nodules with appropriate follow-up, repeat sampling for nondiagnostic/indeterminate results, and refer suspicious or malignant cytology for surgery. Consider surgery for compression, growth, suspicious cytology or patient-specific reasons.

hypothyroidismdiscusscausesclinicaltypes.exp: Causes: primary thyroid failure (Hashimoto thyroiditis, iodine deficiency or excess, thyroidectomy/radioiodine, congenital dysgenesis or dyshormonogenesis, and drugs such as lithium or amiodarone) and central hypothyroidism from pituitary/hypothalamic disease. Types include overt primary, subclinical, central and congenital hypothyroidism. Features include fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry coarse skin/hair, hoarse voice, bradycardia, delayed relaxation of reflexes, menstrual disturbance and nonpitting myxedema. In primary disease TSH is high and free T4 low (subclinical: TSH high, free T4 normal); in central disease free T4 is low with an inappropriately low/normal TSH. Check TPO antibodies when autoimmune thyroiditis is suspected and evaluate pituitary/adrenal function in central disease. Treat with oral levothyroxine, individualized by age, weight and cardiac status; take consistently and separate from iron/calcium. Recheck TSH in about 6–8 weeks after a dose change and adjust; follow free T4 rather than TSH in central hypothyroidism. Treat adrenal insufficiency before starting thyroid hormone when suspected.

femaleladypresentedwithpalpitationlossof.exp: Most likely diagnosis is Graves hyperthyroidism, supported by weight loss, palpitations, anxiety, tremor, staring appearance and diffuse neck swelling. Look for heat intolerance, sweating, increased appetite, frequent stools, diffuse goiter/bruit, lid retraction or lag, proptosis, fine tremor, warm moist skin and hyperreflexia. Measure TSH, free T4 and T3; test TSH-receptor antibodies. Thyroid uptake is diffusely increased in Graves; ultrasound can show diffuse enlargement/hypervascularity. Check ECG for tachyarrhythmia. Relieve symptoms with a beta blocker and treat hormone synthesis with methimazole (PTU in the first trimester of pregnancy); discuss radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy when appropriate, with follow-up thyroid testing.

44yfemaleptpresentedwithfatiguelethargyh.exp: The provisional diagnosis is primary hypothyroidism, likely autoimmune thyroiditis, based on cold intolerance, weight gain, lethargy, bradycardia, puffy face and a thick hoarse voice with goiter/compressive symptoms. Bradycardia causes include hypothyroidism, beta blockers and other rate-limiting drugs, sinus-node disease/heart block, ischemia and high vagal tone. Puffy eyelids may occur with hypothyroidism/myxedema, renal disease, nephrotic syndrome, heart failure or allergy. Confirm with high TSH and low free T4; check TPO antibodies, CBC, lipids and thyroid ultrasound for the neck mass/compression. Anemia may be normocytic, iron-deficiency (including from menorrhagia) or macrocytic from B12/folate deficiency. Ask about menorrhagia, irregular cycles, anovulation, infertility and recurrent pregnancy loss. Hand signs include cool dry skin, delayed relaxation of tendon reflexes, carpal tunnel syndrome, and puffy/nonpitting fingers. Thyroidectomy is considered for significant compressive symptoms, a large goiter, suspicious nodule/cancer, or another structural indication; it is not routine treatment for uncomplicated hypothyroidism.

a23yearoldfemalepatientpresentedwithhist.exp: The likely diagnosis is Graves hyperthyroidism, given weight loss, dyspnea, palpitations, anxiety/insomnia and a family history suggesting autoimmune disease. Other causes include toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis, iodine/amiodarone exposure and exogenous thyroid hormone. Appetite is often increased despite weight loss; menstrual flow may become scant or irregular, with oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea. The most frequent eye sign is upper-lid retraction/stare; assess lid lag, proptosis, conjunctival irritation and restricted eye movements. Hand signs include fine tremor, warm moist palms, palmar erythema, onycholysis and, rarely, thyroid acropachy. Investigations: suppressed TSH, raised free T4 and/or T3, TSH-receptor antibodies; diffuse increased uptake supports Graves, and ultrasound assesses goiter/nodules. ECG is appropriate for palpitations. A beta blocker such as propranolol 20–40 mg every 6 hours controls adrenergic symptoms; methimazole is commonly started at about 10–30 mg/day according to biochemical severity (use PTU in the first trimester of pregnancy). Reassess thyroid function and adjust therapy; discuss definitive treatment if indicated.

21yearsoldstudentfemalecomplainingofirri.exp: The leading possibility is early or mild thyrotoxicosis (including subclinical hyperthyroidism or T3-predominant disease); the absence of a palpable goiter does not exclude it. Repeat TSH and measure free T4 and total/free T3, because TSH is only low-normal; review biotin, thyroid hormone and iodine/amiodarone exposure. If biochemical thyrotoxicosis is confirmed, assess TSH-receptor antibodies and use uptake/scintigraphy or ultrasound according to the suspected cause; obtain an ECG for palpitations. Differential diagnoses include anxiety/panic disorder, stimulant use and pheochromocytoma when clinically suggested. Do not attribute symptoms to a psychiatric disorder before thyroid and relevant medical causes are evaluated. If thyroid testing is normal and symptoms persist, assess for anxiety/depression and arrange psychiatric consultation when indicated.

indicationsofinsulin.exp: Insulin is indicated for all patients with type 1 diabetes; for diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state; for marked symptomatic hyperglycemia or catabolism; when glycemic targets are not reached with non-insulin therapy; and in pregnancy when needed for safe glycemic control.

complicationsofhyperparathyroidism.exp: Complications include renal stones and nephrocalcinosis; bone resorption, bone pain, osteitis fibrosa cystica, and fractures; gastrointestinal symptoms such as constipation, nausea, peptic ulcer disease, or pancreatitis; neuropsychiatric changes; and cardiovascular effects such as hypertension and shortened QT interval.

comparebetween1ry2ryhypoadrenalismcauses.exp: Primary adrenal insufficiency results from adrenal cortical destruction, most often autoimmune, but also from tuberculosis, hemorrhage, infection, metastases, or genetic disease. Cortisol, aldosterone, and adrenal androgens may be deficient. Patients may have fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, salt craving, hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Tests show low cortisol, high ACTH, an inadequate cortisol response to cosyntropin, high renin, and low aldosterone. Treat with glucocorticoid replacement plus fludrocortisone, education about stress dosing, and treatment of the cause. Secondary adrenal insufficiency results from pituitary or hypothalamic disease, surgery, irradiation, or prolonged glucocorticoid suppression. ACTH and cortisol are low or inappropriately normal; aldosterone is usually preserved. Hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia are generally absent, and other pituitary deficits may coexist. Assess ACTH and other pituitary hormones, perform cosyntropin testing as appropriate, and evaluate the pituitary when indicated. Treat with glucocorticoid replacement and address the pituitary cause; fludrocortisone is generally unnecessary.

enumerateriskfactorsofdiabeticnephropath.exp: Risk factors include long diabetes duration, poor glycemic control, hypertension, albuminuria, smoking, dyslipidemia, obesity, and family or genetic susceptibility. Screen with a spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and serum creatinine with estimated GFR: at diagnosis and annually in type 2 diabetes, and beginning five years after diagnosis and annually in type 1 diabetes. Confirm persistent albuminuria with repeat testing. Treatment includes improved glycemic and blood-pressure control, an ACE inhibitor or ARB when hypertension and albuminuria are present, an SGLT2 inhibitor for eligible patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD, lipid management, smoking cessation, and nephrology referral for advanced or progressive disease.

defineprecociouspubertysubclinicalhypoth.exp: Precocious puberty is the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 years in girls or 9 years in boys. Subclinical hypothyroidism is an elevated serum TSH with a normal free T4 concentration. Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of cardiometabolic risk factors, commonly diagnosed when at least three are present: central obesity, elevated triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, elevated blood pressure, and elevated fasting glucose.

mentiononeclinicalbenefitofsgltinhibitor.exp: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart-failure hospitalization and slow progression of diabetic kidney disease in appropriate patients. Carbimazole controls hyperthyroidism by inhibiting thyroid hormone synthesis. GLP-1 receptor agonists improve glycemic control and commonly promote weight loss, with cardiovascular benefit for selected agents. Pioglitazone improves insulin sensitivity and lowers blood glucose in type 2 diabetes.

enumeratemanifestationsofcongenitalhypot.exp: Manifestations include prolonged neonatal jaundice, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, constipation, a hoarse cry, macroglossia, a large or protruding tongue, large fontanelles, umbilical hernia, dry or cool skin, delayed growth, and later developmental delay if untreated.

enumeratetypesclinicalmanifestationsofma.exp: The main types are papillary, follicular, medullary, and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Presentation may include a painless thyroid nodule or goiter, cervical lymphadenopathy, hoarseness, dysphagia, dyspnea, or local invasion. Papillary carcinoma commonly spreads to cervical nodes; follicular carcinoma more often spreads hematogenously to bone or lung; medullary carcinoma may be associated with MEN2 and can cause diarrhea or flushing; anaplastic carcinoma typically causes a rapidly enlarging neck mass with compressive symptoms and a poor prognosis.

Typical laboratory findings include hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, low glucose, and sometimes mild hypercalcemia; primary disease has low cortisol with high ACTH and often high plasma renin with low aldosterone.

indicationsofinsulin.exp: Insulin is essential in type 1 diabetes and is used urgently for diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. It is indicated in type 2 diabetes with marked or symptomatic hyperglycemia, ketosis or catabolism, inadequate control despite appropriate non-insulin therapy, or when other agents are contraindicated or unsuitable. It is also used for diabetes in pregnancy when medication is required, for gestational diabetes not controlled with nutrition and activity, and during severe acute illness, surgery, or critical care when needed for safe glucose control.

caseofhypothyroidismandapproachtodiagnos.exp: Suspect hypothyroidism with fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, hoarse voice, bradycardia, delayed relaxation of reflexes, menstrual disturbance, or goiter, and assess relevant history such as thyroid surgery, radioiodine, neck irradiation, autoimmune disease, and lithium or amiodarone use. Screen with serum TSH in a stable patient with an intact pituitary; an elevated TSH prompts free T4 measurement. Confirm primary overt hypothyroidism with high TSH and low free T4; high TSH with normal free T4 indicates subclinical disease. Low free T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH suggests central hypothyroidism and requires evaluation of other pituitary axes. Identify the cause with thyroid peroxidase antibodies, medication and treatment history, examination, and, when central disease is suspected, pituitary hormone testing and pituitary MRI. Assess for adrenal insufficiency before starting levothyroxine when pituitary disease is possible.

enumeratefunctionaladrenalneoplasms.exp: Functional adrenal neoplasms include cortisol-secreting cortical adenomas or carcinomas causing Cushing syndrome; aldosterone-producing adenomas causing primary aldosteronism; androgen- or estrogen-secreting cortical tumors causing virilization or feminization; and catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary pheochromocytomas. Some cortical tumors can secrete more than one steroid class.

clinicalpictureofghdeficiency.exp: In children, growth hormone deficiency causes reduced height velocity and proportionate short stature, delayed bone age and dentition, a relatively immature facial appearance, and increased central adiposity; intelligence is usually normal. Neonates may have hypoglycemia and boys may have micropenis. In adults, features include reduced lean mass and exercise capacity, increased visceral fat, reduced bone density, adverse lipid changes, fatigue, and impaired quality of life; these findings are nonspecific and require biochemical confirmation.

pituitarycauseshypogonadism.exp: Pituitary causes include prolactinoma or other hyperprolactinemia suppressing hypothalamic GnRH; a nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma compressing gonadotrophs or the stalk; hypopituitarism from pituitary tumors, apoplexy, Sheehan syndrome, trauma, surgery, radiotherapy, infiltrative disease, or hypophysitis; and congenital or genetic pituitary hormone deficiencies. The resulting low LH and FSH cause secondary hypogonadism.

drugcauseshyperprolactinemia.exp: Drugs that can raise prolactin include dopamine D2 antagonists, especially antipsychotics such as risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride, and haloperidol; prokinetics such as metoclopramide and domperidone; some antidepressants; opioids; verapamil; methyldopa; estrogens; and, less commonly, H2 blockers such as cimetidine. Review the medication list and timing before diagnosing a prolactinoma.

causesofpanhypopituitarism.exp: Causes include pituitary macroadenoma or other sellar tumors; surgery or radiotherapy; pituitary apoplexy; postpartum ischemic necrosis (Sheehan syndrome); traumatic brain injury; infiltrative or inflammatory disease such as sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, hemochromatosis, or hypophysitis; metastasis or infection; and congenital or genetic defects affecting the pituitary or hypothalamus. A lesion affecting the gland or stalk can impair multiple anterior pituitary axes; posterior pituitary involvement may also cause diabetes insipidus.

clcomparebetweentype1andtype2diabetesmel.exp: Type 1 diabetes usually begins in childhood or young adulthood and is caused by autoimmune beta-cell destruction, producing absolute insulin deficiency. It often presents abruptly with weight loss or ketoacidosis; islet autoantibodies are often present and C-peptide is low. Type 2 diabetes usually develops gradually, often with central obesity and other insulin-resistance features; insulin resistance is followed by beta-cell dysfunction, C-peptide is initially preserved or high, and islet autoantibodies are absent. For macrovascular prevention: stop smoking, promote regular physical activity and weight control, individualize glycemic targets, control blood pressure, and use statin therapy according to cardiovascular risk. Use antiplatelet therapy for established atherosclerotic disease and, in type 2 diabetes with ASCVD, heart failure, or kidney disease, include a cardioprotective SGLT2 inhibitor and/or GLP-1 receptor agonist when appropriate.

Primary adrenal failure may cause hyponatremia and hyperkalemia; hypoglycemia can occur. Treat immediately: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM, then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours; rapidly give isotonic saline, add dextrose for hypoglycemia, monitor glucose and electrolytes, and treat the precipitating illness. Do not delay treatment for test results. Osteoporosis: often silent until a fragility fracture; vertebral compression fractures cause acute or chronic back pain, height loss, and kyphosis, while hip and distal-radius fractures are other common presentations. Primary hyperparathyroidism: may be asymptomatic or present with renal stones/nephrocalcinosis, bone pain or fragility fractures, muscle weakness, constipation, abdominal discomfort, polyuria/polydipsia, and neurocognitive or mood symptoms. SGLT2-inhibitor adverse effects include genital mycotic infections, volume depletion and hypotension, and rare euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis; counsel about sick-day interruption and perioperative withholding. Causes of thyrotoxicosis include Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis (subacute, painless, or postpartum), excess iodine or amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone, hCG-mediated disease, a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, struma ovarii, and functioning metastatic thyroid carcinoma. Causes of pituitary (secondary) hypogonadism include pituitary tumors or surgery/radiation, Sheehan syndrome or apoplexy, head trauma, infiltrative disease (e.g., hemochromatosis or sarcoidosis), hyperprolactinemia, congenital GnRH deficiency (including Kallmann syndrome), and functional suppression from chronic illness, malnutrition, or excessive exercise.

acausesofshortchildbdiagnosisofdiabetick.exp: Causes of short stature include normal variants (familial short stature and constitutional delay); prenatal growth restriction/small-for-gestational-age birth; malnutrition; chronic renal, gastrointestinal, cardiac, pulmonary, hepatic, or inflammatory disease; endocrine disorders (growth-hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid excess, and poorly controlled diabetes); genetic or chromosomal conditions (e.g., Turner, Noonan, or Down syndrome); skeletal dysplasia; and psychosocial or idiopathic short stature. Diagnose diabetic ketoacidosis when diabetes/hyperglycemia (glucose at least 200 mg/dL or a prior diabetes diagnosis) is accompanied by ketosis (beta-hydroxybutyrate at least 3 mmol/L or urine ketones at least 2+) and metabolic acidosis (venous pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L).

smarksaclassificationsofadrenaltumorsman.exp: Adrenal tumors may be classified by origin as cortical (adenoma or carcinoma) or medullary (pheochromocytoma; extra-adrenal chromaffin tumors are paragangliomas), and by function as hormone-secreting or nonfunctioning. Adrenocortical carcinoma requires hormonal and staging assessment and multidisciplinary care. For localized resectable disease, perform complete en-bloc adrenalectomy with periadrenal tissue, avoiding tumor rupture; use an open oncologic approach when malignancy or invasion is strongly suspected. Consider adjuvant mitotane for high-risk disease; advanced disease may require mitotane-based systemic therapy and selected local treatment. Thyroid: two lateral lobes joined by an isthmus, lying anterior to the trachea and enclosed by pretracheal fascia; Berry ligament anchors it to the larynx/trachea. Important relations are the strap muscles anteriorly, trachea and esophagus medially/posteriorly, recurrent laryngeal nerves in the tracheoesophageal grooves, external branches of the superior laryngeal nerves near the superior thyroid pedicles, and parathyroid glands on the posterior surface. The superior thyroid arteries arise from the external carotids and the inferior thyroid arteries from the thyrocervical trunks; preserve the laryngeal nerves and parathyroids during surgery.

isthispatientneedpsychiatricconsultation.exp:
a) Further symptoms: heat intolerance, weight loss despite increased appetite, palpitation, nervousness/irritability, menstrual irregularity (oligomenorrhoea), muscle weakness. Signs: tachycardia or atrial fibrillation with wide pulse pressure (systolic hypertension), warm moist skin, fine tremor of outstretched hands, lid retraction and lid lag, exophthalmos, diffuse goitre with bruit, proximal myopathy and brisk reflexes, pretibial myxoedema.
b) Most likely diagnosis: thyrotoxicosis, most likely Graves' disease (pheochromocytoma is the main differential of sweating, tremor and hypertension).
c) Investigations: TSH (suppressed), free T4 and free T3 (raised); TSH-receptor antibodies; radioactive iodine uptake scan; thyroid ultrasound; ECG; CBC and liver function tests before treatment; plasma metanephrines if thyroid tests are normal. Treatment: propranolol for symptoms; carbimazole/methimazole for 12-18 months (propylthiouracil in first-trimester pregnancy) with warning about agranulocytosis; definitive radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy for relapse or large goitre; follow-up thyroid function tests.

give2otherpossibilitiesforthiscase1629ye.exp: Two alternative possibilities for a hypothyroid presentation are chronic kidney disease with fluid retention and anaemia, and heart failure; depression or medication effects may also cause fatigue and slowed activity. For the accompanying 29-year-old with sweating, tremor, loose stools and insomnia, thyrotoxicosis (often Graves disease) is likely; assess pulse, goitre, eye and hand signs, TSH, free T4/T3, antibodies and appropriate imaging, then treat with beta blockade and antithyroid medication or definitive radioiodine/surgery. In the 52-year-old insulin-treated diabetic with coma after fever and poor intake, consider hypoglycaemia, DKA and hyperosmolar state. Check bedside glucose, blood gas, ketones, electrolytes, renal function and osmolality, plus infection workup. Treat the identified crisis with glucose rescue or fluids/insulin and potassium-guided care, while treating infection.

44yfemaleptpresentedwithfatiguelethargyh.exp: The likely diagnosis is primary hypothyroidism, probably autoimmune thyroiditis, with possible goitre. Bradycardia causes include hypothyroidism, high vagal tone, sinus node disease, AV block, inferior myocardial infarction, hypothermia, raised intracranial pressure, and drugs such as beta blockers or digoxin. Puffy eyelids may result from hypothyroidism, renal disease, heart failure, allergy, or local inflammation. Confirm with high TSH and low free T4; check thyroid peroxidase antibodies and ultrasound if a goitre or compression needs assessment. Anaemia may be normocytic, iron-deficiency from menorrhagia, or macrocytic from B12/folate deficiency or pernicious anaemia. Ask about menorrhagia, irregular or anovulatory cycles, infertility, miscarriage and reduced libido. Hand signs include cold dry skin, coarse skin, non-pitting swelling, slow relaxation of reflexes, carpal tunnel syndrome, and brittle nails. Surgery is not routine; it may be considered for a large compressive goitre, suspicious nodule, or malignancy.

a23yearoldfemalepatientpresentedwithhist.exp: The most likely diagnosis is Graves disease (autoimmune thyrotoxicosis), supported by weight loss, dyspnoea, palpitations, anxiety, insomnia and a family history. The likely etiology is Graves disease; other causes include toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis, iodine or amiodarone exposure, and exogenous thyroid hormone. Appetite is often increased despite weight loss; menstrual cycles may be scanty or irregular, with reduced fertility. The most sensitive eye sign is lid retraction/lag. Hand signs include warm moist palms, fine tremor, onycholysis, thyroid acropachy, and palmar erythema. TSH is suppressed with raised free T4 and/or T3; TSH-receptor antibodies support Graves disease. Ultrasound may show diffuse enlargement and increased vascularity; uptake scanning shows diffuse increased uptake when indicated. Treat symptoms with a beta blocker and a thionamide (for example carbimazole 15-40 mg daily initially, titrated to response); another class option is propranolol 10-40 mg every 6-8 hours for symptoms. Definitive options are radioiodine or thyroidectomy when appropriate.

an18yearsoldgirlpresentedwithunintention.exp: This is diabetic ketoacidosis, likely new-onset type 1 diabetes. Check bedside and laboratory glucose, venous blood gas, serum bicarbonate and anion gap, blood or urine ketones, electrolytes (especially potassium), urea/creatinine, osmolality, ECG, urinalysis, and cultures or other infection studies when indicated. Begin isotonic IV crystalloid, assess and replace potassium before insulin if potassium is low, then give IV regular insulin with frequent glucose, potassium and ketone monitoring. Add dextrose when glucose falls while continuing insulin until ketoacidosis resolves. Identify and treat the precipitating cause; monitor mental state, fluid balance and cerebral oedema risk.

amalepatient38oldpresentingbyeasyfatigab.exp: The likely diagnosis is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), suggested by postural hypotension, vomiting and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation. Confirm with morning cortisol and ACTH, electrolytes, glucose, plasma renin and aldosterone, and a short Synacthen stimulation test when the patient is stable; ACTH is high and cortisol response is inadequate. Check 21-hydroxylase antibodies and consider adrenal imaging or tests for infection when indicated. In adrenal crisis, draw blood if this does not delay treatment, then give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately followed by 200 mg over 24 hours and rapid isotonic saline, with dextrose if hypoglycaemic. Long-term treatment is oral hydrocortisone in divided doses plus fludrocortisone, sick-day dose education and emergency steroid access.

a17yearsoldfemalepresentedatuniversityho.exp: The likely diagnosis is diabetic ketoacidosis in a patient with previously undiagnosed diabetes. Look for dehydration, Kussmaul respiration, acetone breath, abdominal pain, vomiting, hypotension, tachycardia and altered consciousness. Laboratory findings include hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia/ketonuria, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, low bicarbonate, and total body potassium depletion (serum potassium may initially be normal or high). Treat with isotonic IV fluids, potassium-guided replacement, IV regular insulin, close monitoring and treatment of the precipitant; add dextrose as glucose falls and continue insulin until acidosis/ketosis resolves. whatismostlikelydiagnosis.exp:
1- Most likely diagnosis: thyrotoxicosis without goitre - early Graves' disease, painless (silent/postpartum) thyroiditis, or factitious thyroxine intake; a low-normal TSH alone does not exclude it (T3 toxicosis possible). If thyroid tests prove normal, an anxiety state is the likely diagnosis.
2- Further clinical signs: tachycardia (persisting during sleep in thyrotoxicosis), wide pulse pressure, warm moist hands, fine tremor of the outstretched hands, lid retraction and lid lag, exophthalmos, brisk reflexes, proximal myopathy, weight loss despite good appetite, heat intolerance, frequent stools, oligomenorrhoea.
3- Important investigations: repeat TSH with free T4 and free T3; TSH-receptor antibodies; radioactive iodine uptake/technetium scan (high in Graves', low in thyroiditis or exogenous thyroxine); serum thyroglobulin (low in factitious intake); thyroid ultrasound; ECG; blood glucose; plasma or urinary metanephrines if paroxysmal symptoms with hypertension.
4- Other diagnostic possibilities: anxiety/panic disorder; pheochromocytoma; hypoglycaemia; paroxysmal tachyarrhythmia; drugs (caffeine, sympathomimetics, beta-agonists).
5- Psychiatric consultation: not initially - organic causes (thyrotoxicosis, pheochromocytoma, hypoglycaemia) must be excluded first, because anxiety symptoms are common manifestations of these endocrine disorders; referral is indicated only if all investigations are normal and anxiety symptoms persist.

A) Diagnosis: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) - weight loss, easy fatigability, hyperpigmentation and hypotension.

treatmentduringthehospitalizationtheadvi.exp:
a. Most likely diagnosis: hypoglycaemic coma (insulin-induced hypoglycaemia). Confirmed by capillary (bedside) and laboratory blood glucose below 70 mg/dl (often below 50 mg/dl) and prompt recovery after glucose (Whipple's triad).
b. Explanation: excess insulin relative to glucose intake lowers blood glucose; neuroglycopenia causes impaired consciousness and coma, and the counter-regulatory sympathetic (adrenaline) discharge causes profuse sweating. Other possible clinical features: tachycardia, palpitation, tremor, pallor, hunger, anxiety, headache, confusion, abnormal behaviour, slurred speech, convulsions, focal neurological signs; the skin is moist and breathing is normal (no dehydration or acidotic breathing, unlike DKA).
c. Causes of hypoglycaemia: insulin overdose or error in dose/timing; missed or delayed meals, vomiting; unplanned or strenuous exercise; alcohol; renal failure (reduced insulin clearance); hypoadrenalism or hypopituitarism; malabsorption (coeliac disease); (in non-diabetics: insulinoma, sulfonylurea intake).
d. Therapeutic strategy: immediately IV dextrose (0.5-1 g/kg; e.g. 2-5 ml/kg of 10% dextrose, or 50 ml of 50% in older children) or glucagon 0.5-1 mg IM/SC if IV access is not available; recheck glucose after 15 minutes and repeat if needed; maintain with dextrose infusion then oral complex carbohydrate once conscious; identify the cause and adjust the insulin dose, meal plan and exercise; education of the patient and family about symptoms, carrying sugar, home glucose monitoring, glucagon kit and diabetic identification card.

whatarefurtherclinicalsign.exp:
1) Causes of disturbed consciousness in an insulin-treated diabetic: hypoglycaemic coma; diabetic ketoacidosis; hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state; (also lactic acidosis, cerebrovascular stroke, uraemic coma).
2) Important investigations: immediate capillary blood glucose then laboratory glucose; blood and urine ketones; arterial blood gases (pH, bicarbonate, anion gap); serum sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine; serum osmolality; serum lactate; CBC and cultures for infection; ECG; CT brain if focal neurological signs or no metabolic cause is found.
3) Causes of hypoglycaemia: excessive insulin dose; missed or delayed meals; unaccustomed exercise; alcohol intake; renal or hepatic failure; adrenal insufficiency or hypopituitarism; sulfonylurea use; insulinoma.
4) Clinical signs of middle cerebral artery occlusion: contralateral hemiplegia affecting face and arm more than leg; contralateral hemisensory loss (face and arm); contralateral homonymous hemianopia; conjugate deviation of the eyes toward the side of the lesion; aphasia (Broca's, Wernicke's or global) if the dominant hemisphere is involved; neglect, anosognosia and dressing apraxia if the non-dominant hemisphere is involved.

a. Most likely diagnosis: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) - fatigue, postural dizziness, vomiting, hypotension and recent skin and buccal hyperpigmentation.
b. Causes: autoimmune adrenalitis (commonest; may be part of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome); tuberculosis; other infections (fungal, CMV/HIV); bilateral adrenal haemorrhage (anticoagulants, meningococcal sepsis - Waterhouse-Friderichsen); metastases; infiltration (amyloidosis, haemochromatosis); bilateral adrenalectomy; drugs (ketoconazole, mitotane); congenital adrenal hyperplasia and adrenoleukodystrophy in children and young males.
c. Investigations: 8 a.m. serum cortisol (low) and plasma ACTH (high); short Synacthen test (inadequate cortisol response); serum sodium low, potassium high, urea high, glucose low; plasma renin high, aldosterone low; adrenal autoantibodies; very-long-chain fatty acids in young males; chest X-ray and CT adrenals for tuberculosis or other causes.
d. Endocrinal causes of hyperpigmentation: Addison's disease; ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome, especially ectopic ACTH secretion; Nelson's syndrome (after bilateral adrenalectomy); (also congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hyperthyroidism).
e. Treatment: acute - IV hydrocortisone 100 mg (children about 2 mg/kg) then every 6-8 h, IV normal saline with dextrose, treat the precipitating cause; maintenance - hydrocortisone in divided doses plus fludrocortisone, adequate salt, stress (sick-day) dosing, parenteral hydrocortisone before surgery, steroid card and emergency injection; treat the underlying cause.

giveoneotherdiagnosticpossibility.exp:
1) Most likely diagnosis: primary hypothyroidism (fatigue, loss of libido, constipation, joint pain, puffy face and mild lower limb oedema), most likely autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis.
2) Further symptoms and signs: cold intolerance, weight gain with poor appetite, lethargy and slow mentation, depression, hoarse voice, dry coarse skin, hair loss and loss of the outer third of the eyebrows, menorrhagia, carpal tunnel syndrome, muscle cramps; examination - bradycardia, diastolic hypertension, pallor with yellowish skin, non-pitting oedema, goitre may be present, delayed relaxation of the ankle jerks, pericardial effusion.
3) Investigations to confirm: serum TSH (raised) and free T4 (low); anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies; lipid profile (hypercholesterolaemia), CBC (anaemia), CK, serum sodium; ECG (bradycardia, low voltage); thyroid ultrasound if goitre.
4) Other possibilities: nephrotic syndrome or chronic kidney disease (puffy face, oedema, fatigue); heart failure; depression; rheumatological disease (joint pain with fatigue); hypopituitarism (secondary hypothyroidism with low libido).

give3differentcausesforthispresentation.exp:
a. Most probable 3 D.D.: diabetic ketoacidosis; hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state; hypoglycaemic coma (continuing insulin with loss of appetite) - all precipitated by the febrile infection (also consider sepsis/meningitis and stroke).
b. Expected clinical signs: DKA - dehydration (dry tongue, sunken eyes, hypotension, tachycardia), Kussmaul acidotic breathing, acetone odour of breath, abdominal tenderness; HHS - severe dehydration, no acidotic breathing, focal neurological signs or seizures; hypoglycaemia - sweating, tachycardia, moist skin, normal respiration, possibly convulsions or extensor plantars; plus fever and signs of the infection focus (chest, urine, skin).
c. Investigations and significance: capillary and plasma glucose (low in hypoglycaemia, above 250 mg/dl in DKA, above 600 mg/dl in HHS); blood/urine ketones (high in DKA); arterial blood gases (pH below 7.3 and bicarbonate below 18 in DKA; normal in HHS); serum osmolality (above 320 mOsm/kg in HHS); serum sodium and potassium (guide fluid and potassium therapy); urea and creatinine (prerenal azotaemia); CBC, blood and urine cultures, chest X-ray (source of infection); ECG (hyperkalaemia, silent myocardial infarction).
d. Treatment of one diagnosis (DKA): IV normal saline 1 L in the first hour then according to hydration; IV regular insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/h after K is above 3.3 mmol/L; potassium replacement in the fluids; add 5% dextrose when glucose reaches about 250 mg/dl and continue insulin until ketoacidosis resolves; bicarbonate only if pH below 6.9; antibiotics for the infection; hourly glucose and 2-4 hourly electrolytes and blood gases; then return to subcutaneous insulin overlapping the infusion.
